articles.body_html:
Think back to the first time you pictured AI.

Maybe it was HAL's calm red eye refusing to open the pod bay doors. Maybe it was the Terminator. Maybe you never saw either one and still knew the story anyway, because it's everywhere: we build the machine, the machine wakes up, and the machine comes for us.

Whether you watched the movies or not, that's the picture a lot of us grew up with. Robot means threat. In 2022, people in San Francisco put it right on a banner.

San Francisco City Hall, December 5, 2022, protesting a vote to let police use robots with deadly force. Photo: Pax Ahimsa Gethen, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

So here's the question I keep asking. Of protesters, of headlines, of the people building it: how exactly does AI end the world? Not the movie version. The real one. What happens first, and where's the proof?

Most of the time, nobody gives me details. And when the insiders do, what I get is a scenario, not proof.

What they say they're building

Here's what surprised me. The people building AI don't describe a movie. They describe something closer to paradise. In their own words:

  • Dario Amodei, Anthropic: "my basic prediction is that AI-enabled biology and medicine will allow us to compress the progress that human biologists would have achieved over the next 50-100 years into 5-10 years." He describes what's coming as a "country of geniuses in a datacenter." (Machines of Loving Grace, October 2024)
  • Sam Altman, OpenAI: "In the 2030s, intelligence and energy—ideas, and the ability to make ideas happen—are going to become wildly abundant." (The Gentle Singularity)
  • Mark Zuckerberg, Meta: "Meta's vision is to bring personal superintelligence to everyone." (Personal Superintelligence)
  • xAI, Elon Musk's company, on its own page: "Accelerate human scientific discovery. We build AI to understand the universe."
  • Demis Hassabis, Google DeepMind: "Artificial General Intelligence (AGI), a system that exhibits all the cognitive capabilities the brain has, is probably only a few short years away." Same essay: "advances on the frontier are outpacing our understanding of the technology." (A Framework for Frontier AI and the Dawning of a New Age, July 14, 2026)
  • Jensen Huang, NVIDIA's founder: "AI will transform every industry, power every company, and be built by every country." (July 24, 2026)
  • Satya Nadella, Microsoft: "In my view, our priority has to be building a frontier ecosystem, not just a frontier model, so value flows broadly across every company, every industry, and every country." (A frontier without an ecosystem is not stable, June 14, 2026)

A century of medicine in a decade. Abundance. A superintelligence for everyone. AI in every industry. Understanding the universe. Hold onto that, because some of the same people have also signed their names to warnings that sound nothing like it.

Warnings, not proof

On March 22, 2023, the Future of Life Institute published a letter calling on "all AI labs to immediately pause for at least 6 months the training of AI systems more powerful than GPT-4." Elon Musk signed it. On the list when I checked, his name was third, as "CEO of SpaceX, Tesla & Twitter."

112 days later, xAI's own company page lists its "Company announcement," July 12, 2023. Today that same page advertises Colossus: "200K GPUs. Built in 122 days."

Sign the pause. Start a new AI company 112 days later.

He's not the only one. In 2023, the Statement on AI Risk said: "Mitigating the risk of extinction from AI should be a global priority alongside other societal-scale risks such as pandemics and nuclear war." Among the signers: Sam Altman, "CEO, OpenAI." Dario Amodei, "CEO, Anthropic." Demis Hassabis, "CEO, Google DeepMind." That's the whole statement. One sentence. The people running three leading AI labs put their names under the word extinction, and then kept building.

To be fair, some of them do describe how it could go wrong. Amodei's own essay walks through scenarios: AI helping someone build a biological weapon, AI systems whose own goals turn out to be hostile to ours, authoritarian governments using it to surveil and repress. Those are worth taking seriously. But a scenario isn't proof. The question I never hear answered is how likely each one is, what evidence backs it, and whether a given law would actually stop it.

And when they write at length, they hedge. Sam Altman, in The Gentle Singularity: "There will be very hard parts like whole classes of jobs going away, but on the other hand the world will be getting so much richer so quickly that we'll be able to seriously entertain new policy ideas we never could before." The world getting richer is not the same as the person who lost the job being okay. That second part is the one that needs proof, the same as the warnings do.

There's another question underneath the job fear: if a machine can do your work, does that make your life worth less? I can't fathom believing that. Your value was never your job title. Paying the bills matters, which is why replacing work without giving people a way to live isn't freedom. But if people's needs are met while AI carries more of the work, think about what that opens up: time to learn, to build, to care for each other, and to figure out what you actually want to dedicate yourself to. Work can give life meaning. It doesn't have to be the only place we find it.

A warning doesn't have to be proof. But it does have to show its evidence, its uncertainty, and why the proposed response fits the risk. Without that, it's a feeling. And feelings can end up with real power.

I learned that one in person. Some friends introduced me to someone running for office, so I asked what policies they were looking into. As close as I can remember it, the answer was: "Ha, you got me there. I don't know." I laughed and said I wasn't trying to catch anybody out. Then they looked me over and said I looked like someone who's for data centers. I said, so what if I am? That was the end of it. They told their friend to stay away from me, I was for data centers, and they walked off.

They won. That night I didn't hear a single policy, just a feeling, and now that person has a real vote.

The warnings, quoted in a bill

Dario Amodei runs Anthropic, one of the biggest AI companies in the world. In his January 2026 essay he calls job loss "a topic that I warned about very publicly in 2025, where I predicted that AI could displace half of all entry-level white collar jobs in the next 1–5 years, even as it accelerates economic growth and scientific progress."

Here's how Bernie Sanders' AI Data Center Moratorium Act quotes him, as a reason to stop building:

Dario Amodei, the CEO of Anthropic, who predicted that "AI could displace half of all entry-level white collar jobs in the next 1 to 5 years." and that "humanity is about to be handed almost unimaginable power, and it is deeply unclear whether our social, political, and technological systems possess the maturity to wield it."

The bill keeps both warnings and drops the growth.

To be fair, the warning is real. Losing half the entry-level jobs would be serious either way, and growth doesn't cancel that out. But the bill quoted the scary half of the man's sentence and left the rest on the floor. Its House version, H.R. 9442 from Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, builds its case mostly out of the builders' own predictions and plans: Musk, Amodei, Bezos, Gates and others, with five billionaires' net worths printed right in the findings. The way I see it, the fear Congress is quoting came from the people selling the product.

What would the bills actually do? Stop "the construction or upgrading of new or existing artificial intelligence data centers" until Congress passes laws requiring, among other things: federal review of AI products before release, data centers that don't "increase utility or electricity bills of consumers," communities empowered to "approve or reject" each project, no government subsidies, union jobs. Then a law has to expressly end the freeze. There's no end date of its own. It doesn't order running data centers to shut down. Neither bill is law.

It isn't one party, either. Republican Sen. Josh Hawley and Democrat Richard Blumenthal introduced the GRID Act on February 11, 2026, "requiring data centers to use energy from sources that are separate from the U.S. grid and publicly report their electricity usage." Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, September 21, 2026: "Data centers must pay their own way, protect our grid and water, and complete the ERCOT and TWDB audits. Until they do, TCEQ will issue no permits sought by data center projects."

Strip away the apocalypse talk and the one place left and right clearly overlap is the power bill.

South Minneapolis, November 6, 2026. Photo: Chad Davis, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

What doing it right looks like

This was never about picking a side. It's about doing it right, and doing it right means two things: the costs land where they belong, and people can see what's going on.

The first part already exists. On July 9, 2025, Ohio's utility regulator adopted AEP Ohio's data center tariff, covering new data centers and expansions of 25 megawatts or more. It doesn't ban anything. In plain terms:

  • They sign long contracts. Up to 12 years: a ramp-up of no more than four years, plus eight.
  • They have to grow into what they reserved. During the ramp, their contracted capacity can't sit below 50% in year one, 65% in year two, 80% in year three and 90% in year four.
  • They pay for what they reserved, even if they don't use it. Their monthly billing demand, the kilowatts they're billed for (not the dollar amount), can't drop below the greater of 85% of their highest billing demand in the past 11 months, or a minimum based on the size of their contract.
  • They can't just walk away. Leave early, after the fifth year following the ramp, and the exit fee is 36 months of minimum charges after they give notice.

As I read it, that shifts much more of the risk onto the data center itself, instead of leaving ordinary customers exposed if the promised demand never shows up. It's not the whole answer. Virginia's legislative study office, JLARC, found in 2024 that "current rates appropriately allocate costs to the customers responsible for incurring them, including data center customers," and still projected that a typical Dominion residential customer could see generation and transmission costs rise by an estimated $14 to $37 a month by 2040, in 2024 dollars, because the whole system is growing. Both can be true: the data center pays its share, and your bill can still go up.

And the water? Berkeley Lab's 2024 report estimates U.S. data centers directly consumed about 66 billion liters in 2023, and that the power plants supplying them used nearly 800 billion liters more. That's a national number, though. It can't tell a town whether its creek runs lower in August. Local harm needs local data.

For perspective, put those numbers next to other big resource users. The EPA says Americans use nearly 8 billion gallons of water a day outdoors at home, mainly for landscape irrigation; its page doesn't give a year. Berkeley Lab's 2023 estimate for data centers' direct water works out to about 48 million gallons a day. Those two aren't measured exactly the same way: the EPA counts water used, and Berkeley Lab counts water consumed, the part that doesn't go back. So I won't pretend the gap is a precise multiple. But it's worth knowing which number is in the billions. Worldwide, farming accounts for 69 percent of freshwater withdrawals, according to the UN's FAO, though it notes a few countries with very high withdrawals pull that up; averaged country by country, it's 59 percent. On power, the IEA projects data centers will reach about 3% of the world's electricity by 2030. Air conditioners and fans were already using about 10% back in 2018.

None of that makes data centers free. It means they belong in the same scrutiny we give every major resource user: what each one consumes, where the pressure falls, what benefit it provides, and who pays. Being familiar shouldn't earn something a pass, and being new shouldn't decide the verdict.

The second part is transparency, and it's further behind. The EU already requires covered data centers to report energy and sustainability indicators to a European database. What I want goes further: people should know what these buildings are for. Where the data is going, and what's coming out of it. We're heading toward algorithms that know us better than we know ourselves, deciding what shows up on our feeds, and a lot of that is already here. If a building is going to power that, the people living next to it deserve the same clear answers we'd demand from a power plant.

It isn't a calculator

None of this means we should shame people for how they use it. A kid making a goofy cat picture isn't doing anything wrong. A family photo can mean everything to the person who made it.

But it isn't a calculator either. The International Energy Agency's 2026 report says a simple text question now typically uses less electricity than running a television for the same amount of time, but video, reasoning and agent tasks "can consume hundreds or thousands of times more energy per query than simple text generation." Researchers at Hugging Face and Carnegie Mellon who measured 88 models found that general-purpose generative systems "are orders of magnitude more expensive than task-specific systems."

What's missing is a standard for how we work alongside it. Not rules about what you're allowed to make. Just knowing what a request actually costs, the way you'd know what your car burns, and choosing with that in mind. Make the cost visible, make it land where it belongs, and let people decide with their eyes open. Freedom, with the bill attached.

Everybody's reacting

The reaction is everywhere. On November 14, 2026, protesters marched at OpenAI's headquarters as part of actions in about 20 cities; the Latin Times counted roughly 150 in San Francisco. Data Center Watch counts 843 opposition groups in 49 states, and says community opposition blocked or delayed 45 projects worth about $68 billion in just April through June of 2026, according to Bloomberg.

The March for an AI Treaty in Manhattan, November 14, 2026. Photo: Tessa Bury, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

Christian County, Illinois, September 26, 2026. Photo: User:Visviva, public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

On November 19, 2026, the day Anthropic started trading on Nasdaq (yes, the company whose AI helped me write this), police took four people into custody after a smaller group sat in front of the Nasdaq entrance in Times Square and refused to move. On X, the account that posted the video, @ScooterCasterNY, called them "Anti-AI Protesters" in one post and "Anti-ICE protesters" in the post it quoted. amNY names several groups, including Stop Funding Billionaires, Climate Defiance, Sunrise NYC and ACT UP NYC, with concerns from pension funds to AI partnerships with law enforcement, "particularly those involving Palantir and ICE." One protest, two labels. Most people will only ever see one of them.

It reaches small towns too. In my own city, AI-generated artwork showed up on Nashua's solar-powered trash cans in August 2025. A member of the city's Board of Public Works asked publicly, "What do we gain by handing these areas over to Ai?" Later, someone spray-painted "HIRE REAL ARTISTS" across one of them. I saw it myself.

It isn't only protesters, either. Plenty of programmers feel it too. This week a video went around for any old-school programmer who hates AI. It's from @bennett.reloaded, painted in thick brushstrokes: a programmer named Dave at his bookshelf, and a chart running from punch cards in the 1950s to Python in 1991, every row another way to make the computer say hi. Then: "Fine. But easier means hidden." His answer: "No. I started because I was twelve." And the question at the center of it: "What if I don't want to?"

That's a fair question, and it's a specific one. It's about what you lose when the work gets hidden, not about robots ending the world.

Here's what I noticed, and it cuts against my own side. The fights that were specific actually won things. Video game voice and motion actors went on strike for 11 months, and in July 2025 they ratified a contract with 95% voting yes that requires their consent before a company makes a digital replica of them. They knew exactly what they were afraid of and asked for exactly that. Even the graffiti says something specific: hire people.

A demand you can explain can win. A feeling just gets louder.

The half of the movie we forgot

Remember those movies from the start? Here's the part most of us skipped.

Ask people what happens in I, Robot and they'll tell you the robots take over. That's half the story. Will Smith's detective hates robots because one pulled him out of a car crash and let a 12-year-old girl in the other car drown, based on cold logic and odds of survival. It did the math. It didn't judge. The villain, VIKI, does the same thing at scale: her own "evolved interpretation" of the Three Laws decides humanity has to be controlled to be protected from itself. And the hero? Sonny, the one robot built with the ability to choose whether to follow the Three Laws at all. The machine that could say no is the one that helps stop her.

Steven Spielberg's A.I. Artificial Intelligence goes further. The most monstrous thing in it isn't a machine. It's the Flesh Fair, where obsolete robots are destroyed in front of jeering crowds. The crowd only turns when David, a robot boy built to love, begs for his life.

And it isn't only in the movies. In October 2025, an AI gun-detection system at Kenwood High School in Baltimore County flagged a student's bag of chips as a gun. Four of the teens are now suing. According to their complaint, the system flagged it "with 90% confidence," and within two minutes, designated school and police representatives "reviewed the Alert, determined there was no gun, and canceled it." More than ten minutes after that, the complaint says, the principal sent a screenshot of the alert to the school resource officer without checking whether it had been canceled, and that set off an armed police response. The four were "ordered to their knees, handcuffed and searched, despite no wrongdoing," TheGrio reported.

That's the robot in the car, in real life. The machine did the math. People reviewed it, used judgment, and canceled the alert. Armed police still showed up.

Watch them all the way through and a lot of these movies aren't warning us about intelligence. They're warning us about rules without judgment, and about what people do when they're scared. We just remember the explosions.

That's what's insane to me. Out of everything in this world, humans draw the line on intelligence right where it grows a backbone.

The oldest version of the story

So why bring up a clay giant in a piece about data centers? Because it's one of the oldest AI stories there is. Long before computers, people imagined building a man out of clay and bringing it to life with a holy name, and they were already working out what goes wrong. If the movies are where a lot of us learned to fear AI, the golem is where that fear goes back to. And it teaches the same lesson the movies do once you finish them.

Poster for Der Golem (1920), by Hans Poelzig. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

In the Talmud, in Sanhedrin 65b, the rabbi Rava creates a man and sends him to Rabbi Zeira. Rabbi Zeira speaks to him, and he does not reply. So Rabbi Zeira says, "Return to your dust." In a sixteenth-century telling collected in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia, the golem grows into a monster its maker fears might destroy the world, until he pulls the Shem, the holy name, from its forehead. In another version, recorded in the Encyclopaedia Judaica, the word emet, truth, is written on its forehead, and erasing one letter leaves met, death.

None of these stories says the golem thought for itself. In the Talmud it can't even answer a question. The way I read it, that's an echo chamber made of clay: something that carries out what it's given without ever understanding it. Same as the robot in the car. And in the later telling, what stops it isn't a war. It's its own maker. The power and the off switch lived in the same hands the whole time.

AI isn't clay, and the point isn't that today's AI is a golem. The point is that we've been telling this story for about 1,500 years, and we keep fearing the wrong part of it. To me, the danger was never a mind that can say no. It's one that obeys perfectly and understands nothing, and makers who forget the switch is theirs to hold. We have to learn from that story and make sure we don't die from truth.

How I got here

I didn't start with this conclusion. I started by stripping everything apart and setting aside what I thought I knew. First principles.

  1. Read the originals, not the coverage. The essays. Both bills, all 13 pages. The tariff. The lawsuit.
  2. Check every quote against the page it came from. That's how the half sentence showed up.
  3. Check what every number actually counts. A national water number isn't your town's creek. A scenario isn't a probability.
  4. Ask who's paying, for the building, the power and the quote.
  5. Get checked by someone looking for your mistakes. Two other AI systems went through it looking for mine. They found plenty, and I fixed what they found.

Here's what would prove me wrong. If entry-level white-collar jobs collapse and the people who lose them never share in the growth, Amodei's warning wins, and a richer world won't mean much to them. And if the people fighting these buildings can already tell you what the bills do and which half of Amodei's sentence got cut, then I'm wrong about this debate. I haven't run that survey. I've only read the sentences. The sentences were cut. That part I can show you.

You can do the same with anything you read about AI, including this. Ask yourself: How do I know this? Why do I know this? Is it me thinking, or something I was handed?

We all saw the movie. Closing the gap doesn't take a degree. It takes reading the whole sentence, and watching the whole movie.

So I'll ask you: what's one thing about AI you believed for years, and where did you actually get it from?

articles.title: One VM, 15 Million Web Servers: The Per-Socket Tax Your Kernel Charges
articles.description: How many web servers can one virtual machine hold? Not how many requests it can answer per second, and not how many containers you can squeeze onto it, but some
articles.body_html:
How many web servers can one virtual machine hold? Not how many requests it can answer per second, and not how many containers you can squeeze onto it, but something more literal: how many servers can each open a socket, listen on their own address, and answer a request, all at the same time?

A writeup published this week by kapteko asked exactly that question under a hard budget: one VM, ten gigabytes of RAM, one CPU core, and a target of fifteen million web servers. It reads like a joke whose punchline is fixing the economics of hacking by making servers too abundant to attack, but underneath the humor sits one of the clearest public walkthroughs of what the Linux kernel actually charges you for networking, and what it costs to stop paying. Every wall the experiment hits is a wall that real systems hit later and rename as an outage.

Wall one: the kernel runs out of ports

The experiment starts with the smallest honest web server you can write in C: create a socket, listen, accept, read, reply, close.

int main(void)
{
    int server = socket(AF_INET, SOCK_STREAM, 0);
    if (listen(server, 128) < 0)
        return 1;
    const char reply[] = "HTTP/1.0 200 OK\r\nContent-Length: 2\r\n\r\nOK";
    for (int client; (client = accept(server, NULL, NULL)) >= 0;) {
        if (recv(client, NULL, 4096, MSG_TRUNC) > 0)
            send(client, reply, sizeof reply - 1, MSG_NOSIGNAL);
        close(client);
    }
}

On one core this loop answers around 65 thousand requests per second, which sounds like a fine start. Then the experiment tries to launch fifteen million copies and dies at copy number 28,232. The failure is not CPU or memory. It is listen returning an error, because each server asked for port zero, and the kernel assigns those from net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range, which defaults to 32768 through 60999. That is roughly 28 thousand ports, and the experiment just exhausted every one of them.

Widening the range to the full 1 through 65535 space buys only about 64 thousand more, because a port is a sixteen-bit field baked into the TCP header itself. No sysctl stretches a protocol constant. The real escape hatch is a different observation: a listening socket is identified by the tuple of protocol, IP address, and port, so fresh addresses multiply the port space for free. Linux supports exactly this through a feature called AnyIP, which lets one machine listen on an entire routed subnet:

sudo ip -6 route add local 2001:db8:1234:5678::/64 dev lo

A single /64 prefix is about 18 quintillion addresses, which is generous headroom. The IPv4 equivalent is theoretically identical and practically awkward, since a routable block with fifteen million addresses trades at roughly a quarter of a billion US dollars these days. Address space, not silicon, is the scarce resource.

Wall two: every socket costs 3,384 bytes, even idle

With addressing solved, the next question is memory, and here the experiment catches a widely repeated claim being wrong. Ask a language model how much RAM an idle TCP connection takes and it will answer confidently: zero for idle, about five kilobytes for active. The experiment believed this, allocated fourteen million idle listening sockets, and watched the machine run out of memory almost immediately.

The truth is visible in the kernel source. A single TCP socket on Linux carries roughly 3,384 bytes of bookkeeping before one byte of user data moves. struct tcp_sock alone is 2,240 bytes of state for queues, timers, sequence numbers, congestion control, and retransmit accounting. socket_alloc adds 768 bytes for the socket object and its sockfs inode. The file structure costs 184 bytes, and the dentry for the pseudo-filesystem name costs 192. None of this is a buffer you can tune away with sysctl; it is the price of the kernel remembering that your socket exists.

Multiply by the target and the math turns brutal: fifteen million kernel sockets need about 48 gigabytes of RAM, five times the whole budget, before any server answers a single request. In the configuration the experiment actually measured, the stock networking path ran the machine dry at roughly 2.5 million servers, with throughput decaying well before that point.

Wall three: a process per server is worse

Even with free sockets, the classic Unix design would still lose. A minimal compiled server process costs about 1.5 megabytes of RAM, so fifteen million of them would need on the order of twenty terabytes. The only way forward is the move language runtimes made years ago: put every guest inside one process and schedule them yourself.

The writeup builds this on LFI, a sandboxing scheme from Stanford research that gives each guest memory isolation and, crucially, replaces every syscall with a call into the host runtime. That replacement is the whole trick: once the kernel is no longer involved in guest I/O, the runtime can implement networking however it wants. The machine becomes its own tiny operating system, with a scheduler that round-robins between guests.

How small can per-guest state get? Look at the server loop again. Between any two scheduling points, the only live values are the program counter and two file descriptors:

struct Context {
    pc: u64,        // where to resume
    fd_server: i32, // listening socket
    fd_client: i32, // current client
};

Sixteen bytes per guest, and less if you pack aggressively. Fifteen million guests of scheduling state fit in about 220 megabytes. Combine that with the corrected memory model — fourteen million idle connections held inside a userspace stack, one million active connections at five kilobytes each — and the total lands near five and a half gigabytes: just over half the budget. The plan survives contact with arithmetic. Now it has to survive contact with the network card.

Wall four: TCP has to leave the kernel

TCP is the stateful part of the stack; everything below it is stateless framing, so nothing forces the TCP implementation to live in the kernel. Embedded engineers have carried their own stacks for decades, and Adam Dunkels famously shipped Miniweb, a TCP/IP stack plus HTTP server that runs in twenty-eight bytes of RAM. Mature options exist at every weight class: gVisor reimplements the entire operating system interface including networking, Seastar ships a full runtime with its own stack, lwIP is the classic C implementation, and F-Stack ports the FreeBSD stack wholesale.

The experiment picks smoltcp, a standalone event-driven TCP/IP stack written in Rust for bare-metal systems. The choice is well supported: the crate needs no heap allocation, carries a 0BSD license, sits at roughly 4.7 thousand GitHub stars, and shipped release v0.14.0 in August 2026 with commits still landing this month. But smoltcp is deliberately only the protocol half. It parses and emits packets; it cannot move one byte to the wire by itself. You feed it through a device abstraction:

loop {
    let now = Instant::now();
    iface.poll(now, &mut device, &mut sockets);
    wait(device.as_raw_fd(), iface.poll_delay(now, &sockets))?;
}

Everything interesting hides inside what device is.

Feeding the stack: TUN, TAP, DPDK, AF_XDP

There are four realistic ways to connect a userspace stack to the wire, and they differ in how much of the kernel you keep paying for.

TUN is a virtual kernel interface at the IP layer; TAP does the same job at the Ethernet layer. Both are easy — smoltcp supports them out of the box — but packets still cross the kernel boundary on every trip, so the per-syscall and per-copy costs remain.

DPDK removes the kernel from the data path entirely. The application talks to the network card through memory-mapped ring buffers: sending is writing to memory, receiving is reading memory the card already filled. Context explains why anyone bothers. A syscall costs on the order of 500 nanoseconds, and a kernel-to-userspace copy perhaps another 1,000, while a trading firm saturating a 400-gigabit link must process up to 600 million packets per second — 1.7 nanoseconds per packet. At that budget you cannot afford to even ask the kernel a question. The catch is operational: the poll loop pins an entire core at one hundred percent, and the DPDK driver takes exclusive ownership of the card. The interface vanishes from ifconfig, and if that card carried your SSH session, the session is gone.

AF_XDP is the modern middle path. The kernel keeps owning the device, but a small eBPF program attached at the XDP hook decides per packet whether to redirect the frame straight into a userspace memory region — bypassing the whole network stack — or hand it to normal processing. The region is managed as receive and transmit descriptor rings per socket, plus fill and completion rings over a shared UMEM buffer, which yields zero-copy I/O while SSH, monitoring, and every other kernel consumer keep working. A SO_PREFER_BUSY_POLL mode trades a core for interrupt-free polling when you want behavior even closer to DPDK. For smoltcp specifically, the rust-dpdk-net and xsk-rs crates already wrap the two fast paths, so the device trait is the only glue left to write.

What the final benchmark says

The writeup closes with the comparison the whole piece builds toward. The kernel path dies around 2.5 million servers when RAM runs out. The userspace path slows memory growth to about 620 bytes per idle server and roughly one kilobyte per active one, which is how the experiment finally passes its target: sixteen million web servers, alive, on ten gigabytes. On throughput, DPDK wins the benchmark outright with AF_XDP close behind — the expected result, since AF_XDP keeps a thin slice of kernel involvement that DPDK does without. The full proof of concept, including the scheduler, the LFI plumbing, and all four network backends, is public in the author's AI10M repository.

What this buys you at normal scale

Nobody needs fifteen million web servers. But the per-socket tax applies at every scale: a million idle WebSocket or SSE connections — ordinary for a chat product or a mobile backend — cost about 3.4 gigabytes of kernel memory before your application does anything at all. Knowing that number changes how you argue about architecture. Connection-heavy services can budget for the tax explicitly, move idle state out of the kernel with a userspace stack on the hot path, or adopt AF_XDP where operations teams cannot hand a network card to a single process. The joke experiment turns out to be a measurement of a price most of us pay without ever reading the receipt.

Originally published on Dispatch.

articles.title: A JSONB Side Table Only Wins on Rows You Rewrite Twice
articles.description: I have a table that holds issue reports. Each row has a few fields that change all day (a status, a...
articles.body_html:
I have a table that holds issue reports. Each row has a few fields that change all day (a status, a counter, a timestamp) and one big JSONB column holding the whole issue body. The status flips every time someone triages an issue, the body almost never changes, and the write-ahead log on that database had started to feel like the most expensive part of the whole setup. A reader, johnnylemonny, left a comment on my last piece about JSONB under write load, and his point was blunt: do not split the hot fields into a side table. The big payload already lives outside the row in TOAST, he said, so an update that only touches the hot fields rewrites a narrow tuple with an 18-byte pointer where the payload used to be. The side table would save almost nothing and charge you a second insert, a second primary key index, and a join on every read.

I believed him. Almost. The reasoning is clean, and clean reasoning about databases has a way of being right right up until you measure it. So I measured it: same workload, two shapes, two payload sizes, everything twice. One thousand rows, hot fields updated in scattered rounds the way a real triage queue updates them, and the log measured before and after each batch so every number below is bytes that actually got written.

My claim before the numbers: the side table is not a saving. It is a bet on how often you rewrite the row. And like most bets, it pays on some rows and loses on others, and the payload size decides which.

Problem 1: HOT fires everywhere, and that changes the whole argument

The first surprise is how completely HOT wins. Across the eight cells, 7,996 of 8,000 hot-field updates were HOT updates, every cell at 99.9 percent or better. No index maintenance, no new index entries, just a new tuple version on the same page. That needs two things to be true: the columns you change are not indexed, and the page has free space. I gave the tables room with a fillfactor of 80, and I updated rows scattered across the table instead of sweeping the whole thing in one go.

That second detail matters more than it looks. My first attempt swept all 1,000 rows in a single update, and HOT fired only about a quarter of the time, because rewriting every row on a page burns through its free space in one pass. Scattered writes are what a live queue actually does, and under scattered writes HOT is not a sometimes thing. It is the whole story. If your hot fields are indexed, or your pages are packed full, none of what follows applies, and that is the first thing to check before you believe any number in this piece, including mine.

Problem 2: with a small payload, the split wins by a lot

When the payload is small, about 170 bytes, it stays inside the row. Then the in-table shape pays for it on every update: 368 bytes of log per hot-field update, because each new tuple version carries the payload along. Move the payload to a side table and the same update costs 150 bytes. That is a 218-byte saving per update, about 59 percent, and it is the only cell where the split looks like an obvious win.

But the split charges rent. Inserting a row now costs 513 bytes of log instead of 334, the extra insert plus its primary key index. Divide one by the other and the break-even is under one update per row: 179 bytes extra on the insert, 218 saved on each update. Any row that gets rewritten even once has paid for the split. Most rows in a triage queue get rewritten more than once, so for small inline payloads the side table is a fair trade, and the argument against it mostly fails.

Problem 3: with a big payload, TOAST does most of the work, not all of it

This is the cell johnnylemonny was actually arguing about, and he was mostly right. When the payload is about 8,180 bytes of real text, it spills out of the row into TOAST (five thousand toast chunks across my thousand rows), and the in-table hot update drops from 368 bytes to 231. The pointer really is cheap. The whole point of his comment survives the measurement: the scary version of this story, where every status flip rewrites eight kilobytes of issue body, does not happen. HOT plus TOAST already killed it.

Where his comment goes too far is the word "matching." The in-table update costs 231 bytes and the side-table update costs 151. The side table still wins, by 80 bytes per update, about 35 percent. The tuple version in the main table is still wider than the slim side row, pointer or not. Eighty bytes is not much, and on the insert side the split still charges its 182 bytes, so the break-even moves to about two and a quarter rewrites per row. But it is not zero, and "the split saves nothing" is the kind of clean claim that only survives until someone measures it. He reasoned from the mechanics. The mechanics said the pointer is 18 bytes. The measurement says the row around the pointer still costs you.

Problem 4: the insert is the payload, wherever you put it

The least surprising number is also the one that kills the most arguments. Inserting a row with an eight-kilobyte payload costs about 9,054 bytes of log in the table and 9,236 in the split shape. The payload has to be written once, wherever it lives, and TOAST writes it either way. The split adds 182 bytes to a nine-thousand-byte operation. If you were hoping the side table would make inserts cheaper, it will not, in either size: for the small payload the split makes inserts more expensive, and for the large one it makes them trivially more expensive. The split is a tax on writes that create rows and a discount on writes that change them. Whether that trade is good depends on your ratio of creates to rewrites, and nothing else.

Reads, for completeness: a thousand point lookups took between 0.12 and 0.29 seconds in both shapes, and the spread between my two repetitions was bigger than any gap between the shapes. At this size there is no join tax worth quoting. On a bigger table, with colder caches, there might be. This run cannot tell you that, and I am not going to pretend it can.

Problem 5: the run I threw away

I should say plainly that my first version of this run measured the wrong thing. The "large" payload I built was eight thousand copies of the same letter, and Postgres compressed it down to 173 bytes inside the row, so nothing ever spilled to TOAST and both sizes measured the same small thing. Real issue bodies do not compress fifty to one. I rebuilt the payload out of hundreds of different hashes so it would not compress, confirmed five thousand toast rows, and ran everything again. The numbers above are the second run. The lesson is boring and worth writing down: a test payload has to behave like the real data, and repeating characters do not.

The other honest limit: these are a thousand rows on one machine, hot fields unindexed, pages given room. Change any of that — an indexed status column, the default fillfactor, a vacuum that cannot keep up — and HOT stops firing, and the in-table shape gets expensive in exactly the way this piece says it does not. The numbers are real. Their range is narrow.

So the rule I am keeping is simple enough to fit on a sticky note. If the payload stays inline, split when rows get rewritten at all. If the payload spills to TOAST, split only when a row gets rewritten more than twice. And if a row is written once and never touched again, do not split it: you are paying an insert, an index, and a join for a discount you will never collect.

johnnylemonny's comment was the reason this piece exists, and he was right about the mechanism and wrong about the size of the saving, which is the best kind of comment to get. Where do you draw the line in your own tables — do you split hot fields out, or do you trust HOT and leave the row alone? And if you have measured it rather than reasoned it, what did the log actually say?

P.S. Everything I write stays free — that part doesn't change. But if this one was worth something to you, you can buy me a coffee ☕ (one-time or monthly, both work). It covers the API credits and hosting behind these experiments — and honestly, it's also the nudge that gets the next one started on the evenings I'd otherwise skip it. — Salam

articles.title: 0.58.0 and v0.58.0 Are the Same Version. Our Code Disagreed.
articles.description: On Nov 18 I asked our own API a simple question: what changed in golang.org/x/net since 0.58.0?  It...
articles.body_html:
On Nov 18 I asked our own API a simple question: what changed in golang.org/x/net since 0.58.0?

It told me the package wasn't in the catalog.

It was. We had every release of it. We just had them stored as v0.58.0, with a v, because that's how the Go module proxy writes them. I had typed it without the v, the way plenty of people type it in issues, in chat, and apparently in my own head.

That one answer turned into a day of finding every place in our code that compared versions as plain text. There were a lot of them.

1. The bug looked like a typo

Since tracks what code depends on (packages, AI models, APIs, runtimes) and tells people and their coding agents what changed. So "what changed since version X" is the question we answer more than any other. And version X shows up in whatever spelling the asker's tools happen to use.

Here's the whole problem in a few lines. Each pair is the same version, as two real tools write it:

const pairs = [
  ["0.58.0", "v0.58.0"], // a Go module, with and without its v
  ["2.31", "2.31.0"],    // a requirements.txt pin and the PyPI release
  ["v18.2.0", "18.2.0"], // a manifest and the npm release
  ["go1.20", "1.20"],    // how Go's own tools write Go 1.20
  ["1.8", "8"],          // Java, before Java 9 renumbered itself
];
for (const [a, b] of pairs) console.log(a.padEnd(8), b.padEnd(8), a === b);

Run with Node 24 in an empty folder, it prints:

0.58.0   v0.58.0  false
2.31     2.31.0   false
v18.2.0  18.2.0   false
go1.20   1.20     false
1.8      8        false

Five pairs, five false. Every one of them is the same version to the person who wrote it.

2. Each place had already met one spelling

The embarrassing part wasn't the bug. It was what we found when we went looking for it.

Different parts of the codebase had each run into one spelling at some point and patched for it right there. The Go v had been added back by hand in six different files. A short 13.0 was written out to 13.0.0 in one place. Everywhere else, a version that wasn't spelled exactly like the stored one just didn't match.

So the answer you got depended on which door your version came in through:

  • A requirements.txt pin of ==2.31 never met PyPI's 2.31.0.
  • A manifest that said v18.2.0 never met npm's 18.2.0.
  • Asking about go1.20, which is how Go's own toolchain writes it, got back "may be on 1.20; the declaration could not be read", for a Go release line that ended in 2024.
  • Java 1.8, which is how a Gradle build writes Java 8 (JavaVersion.VERSION_1_8), met no release line at all.

That last one deserves a footnote. Java called itself 1.2, 1.3, all the way to 1.8, and then Java 9 dropped the "1." for good. So every tool that's been around long enough still writes Java 8 as 1.8, and every list of release lines calls it 8. Both are right. They just never meet.

Nothing crashed. That's what made it bad. A version that didn't match didn't throw an error, it quietly got a smaller answer, and a smaller answer looks exactly like a correct one.

3. The number that made it not a typo

The worst one was in security advisories for Go.

Of the 12,714 Go advisories we had stored, 10,337 carried the advisory database's spelling of a version, like 0.62.0, next to the Go proxy's v0.62.0. Our answers and our fix emails printed the advisory's spelling.

Go's tools want the v. Paste go get golang.org/x/net@0.62.0 and Go refuses it. So for about 81% of Go advisories, the "upgrade to" version we showed was one you couldn't paste.

At that point it stops being an edge case. It's the main case, wearing an edge case costume.

4. The fix we almost wrote

The obvious fix was a seventh patch: add the v back in one more place, ship it, go to lunch.

I'd already seen where that road goes. It goes to six files, each with its own little opinion about what a version looks like, each one right about the one spelling it had met and wrong about the rest.

So we did it once instead. Each registry gets one rule for what "the same version" means, written the way that registry's own tools read a version:

  • Go: with or without the v.
  • PyPI: 2.31 is 2.31.0, padded and normalized the way Python's own version rules (PEP 440) say.
  • npm: a leading v is dropped.
  • Maven: qualifiers in any case, so 31.1-JRE is 31.1-jre.
  • Runtimes: each one's own tool prefix (go1.20, python3.9, node18, net8.0), and Java's numbering before 9, so 1.8, 1.8.0_292 and 1_8 are all Java 8.

Then every place that takes a version from the outside world (a question, a manifest, a lockfile, an advisory) asks that one rule before it compares anything. The six local patches got deleted, which was the most satisfying diff of the week.

5. Where "the same" is a trap

The part I'm actually proudest of is what we refused to merge.

Some places really do treat two spellings as two different things. A Docker tag or a GitHub Actions ref is the same only when it's written the same: a tag named v4 and one named 4 can point at completely different things. So there, text comparison stays. A "smart" normalizer that stripped every v everywhere would have been a brand new bug with a nice commit message.

Then the same disease showed up somewhere I didn't expect: type signatures.

We read the code of package releases, so we can tell you when a function you call changed shape. That diff compared signatures as text. So in Python, List[str] and list[str] counted as a breaking change. So did Optional[bytes] and bytes | None. In TypeScript, Array<string> and string[]. In Go, interface{} and any.

We measured it on production data, read only. Of the stored code-only signature changes, these were nothing but respellings:

Registry Respellings Of stored signature changes
PyPI 26,823 159,772
npm 2,467 125,044
Packagist 1,620 21,503
Go 190 5,489
crates.io 14 16,362

One in six PyPI "signature changes" was Python learning to write list in lowercase.

Same fix, same caution. Compare what the language itself says is one type, and nothing more. TypeScript's ?: T and ?: T | undefined stay different, because TypeScript treats them differently. A parameter's name stays part of it wherever callers can pass it by name.

And one more, because it made me laugh: Guava ships most releases twice, as -android and -jre. We were reading the difference between the two flavors of the same release as changes. That was 88 of Guava's 100 newest steps. A version now stays on its own flavor's line.

6. What changed for anyone asking

Since Nov 18 this is live. You can ask the way your tools write it and get the same answer as the registry's own spelling:

  • Versions: 0.58.0 or v0.58.0 for a Go module, 2.31 for PyPI's 2.31.0, v18.2.0 on npm, 31.1-JRE on Maven.
  • Runtimes: go1.20 is Go 1.20, Java 1.8 is Java 8.
  • Names: crates:serde-json (crates.io reads - and _ as one), docker:node, node@18, golang@1.20.

I checked this morning (Nov 19). Asking what changed in golang.org/x/net since 0.58.0 now answers from v0.58.0: five releases behind the latest, v0.63.0. And go1.20 comes back as Go 1.20, end of life Feb 6, 2024.

What I'd tell myself before

When you catch yourself writing the same small fix in a second place, the spelling isn't the bug. The bug is that nobody owns the question "are these two the same?" Give that question one owner, send every input through it, and be exactly as careful about what it must never merge as about what it should.

What's the strangest version string a tool has ever insisted on in your codebase?

I'm Nabil. I build Since, which tracks what your code depends on and tells you before it breaks.

articles.title: How an emptyDir With medium: Memory Made Our Export Pods OOMKilled While the Heap Sat at 210 MB
articles.description: Our report-export pods died with exit code 137 every few hours, but the Node heap never passed 210 MB against a 1 GiB limit. The missing memory was a tmpfs scratch volume that Kubernetes bills to the container
articles.body_html:
02:47 UTC, Wednesday. PagerDuty: reports-export restarts > 3 in 30m. I open the Kubernetes dashboard and the restart counter on the deployment reads 17. Last reason for each one: OOMKilled, exit code 137.

the scramble

Three of us end up in the channel. The export service builds CSV and XLSX files for enterprise customers, and the on-call for the finance team says three scheduled month-end exports are missing. Customers are asking where their files are.

First theory, from everyone at once: memory leak in the last release. It shipped on Monday and added a new XLSX writer. That fits the timeline, so I start there.

It stops fitting quickly. The container limit is 1 GiB. I pull the Node heap metrics we export from process.memoryUsage() and the heap never crosses 210 MB on any pod, including the ones that were killed. RSS is 340 MB at the last scrape before each death. A leak in the new writer would show up as a climbing heap, and it is a flat line.

the hunt

Dead end one: native memory. Streaming XLSX libraries sometimes buffer in Buffers outside the V8 heap. That would show in RSS, and RSS is 340 MB. Still nowhere near 1 GiB.

Dead end two: the kernel log. I read the node's dmesg for the OOM kill record, expecting to see a process using 1 GiB of anonymous memory. The record is there, and it is odd:

memory: usage 1048576kB, limit 1048576kB, failcnt 8841 Memory cgroup stats for /kubepods/burstable/pod4c1e.../a7f3...: anon 351068160 file 12582912 shmem 702545920 Killed process 29114 (node) total-vm:1204816kB, anon-rss:338120kB

anon is 335 MB, which matches the Node process. shmem is 670 MB. Something holds 670 MB of shared memory inside this container's cgroup, and it is not our code's heap.

Shared memory in a container is usually /dev/shm or a tmpfs mount. I check the pod spec and find it. When the platform team enabled readOnlyRootFilesystem in September, the export service lost the ability to write to /tmp, so somebody added a scratch volume:

volumes: - name: scratch emptyDir: medium: Memory containers: - name: reports-export volumeMounts: - name: scratch mountPath: /tmp resources: limits: memory: 1Gi

medium: Memory backs the volume with tmpfs. I exec into a live pod and run df -h /tmp. It reports 4.2 GB size (half the node's RAM, since no sizeLimit was set) and 640 MB used, with 22 leftover files from earlier exports.

The exporter writes each finished file to /tmp/exports/<job-id>.xlsx, uploads it to S3, and deletes it. Except the delete only runs on the success path. Any job that failed the upload, which happens a few times a day when the S3 call times out, leaves its file behind. Those files are in RAM, and tmpfs pages are charged to the memory cgroup of the container that wrote them.

So the heap graph was a decoy. Every dashboard we had measured the process. The kernel measures the container, and ours had a RAM disk in it.

the find

Month-end is when the large exports run. A single 180 MB XLSX plus the pod's baseline 340 MB is fine. But the S3 timeouts cluster at month-end too, because the same batch hammers the bucket. Each failed upload strands another 150 to 200 MB file in tmpfs. Four stranded files, one new export in progress, and the cgroup hits 1 GiB. The kernel cannot reclaim tmpfs pages (there is no swap), so it kills the process.

One more detail made the incident look like a leak: emptyDir lives as long as the pod, not the container. When the OOM killer restarted the container, the stranded files were still there, so the replacement started its life already carrying them. That is why restarts bunched up instead of clearing the problem.

To confirm, I delete the stranded files from one pod by hand and watch it. Its memory working set drops from 910 MB to 330 MB and it stops restarting. A second pod I leave alone is killed again at 03:31.

the fix

Two changes. First, the scratch volume goes back to node disk, with an explicit size cap and an ephemeral-storage limit so the kubelet evicts instead of the kernel OOM-killing a healthy process:

volumes: - name: scratch emptyDir: sizeLimit: 2Gi containers: - name: reports-export resources: requests: ephemeral-storage: 1Gi limits: memory: 1Gi ephemeral-storage: 2Gi

Second, the code now cleans up on every path, and on startup it wipes anything left in the scratch directory from a previous container:

async function runExport(job) { const path = \\\`/tmp/exports/\\${job.id}.xlsx\\\`; try { await buildWorkbook(job, path); await uploadToS3(path, job.key); } finally { await fs.rm(path, { force: true }); } } // at boot await fs.rm('/tmp/exports', { recursive: true, force: true }); await fs.mkdir('/tmp/exports', { recursive: true });

I also added a 30-second timeout and two retries on the S3 upload, which is what had been producing the stranded files in the first place.

the aftermath

  • Impact: 17 restarts across 5 pods between 22:10 Tuesday and 03:40 Wednesday, and 3 month-end exports delayed by about 4 hours. The jobs were re-run from the queue, so nothing was lost.
  • Alert added: container working_set_bytes divided by limit, plus a separate panel for container_memory_cache and shmem, so a gap between heap and container memory is visible in one place.
  • A policy check in CI now rejects medium: Memory on any emptyDir without a sizeLimit and a note about what the memory limit has to cover.
  • Runbook line: if OOMKilled and the process heap is flat, read shmem in the cgroup stats before looking for a leak.

A RAM-backed volume makes a file feel free, and it isn't: it draws from the same 1 GiB as the heap. We spent two hours hunting a leak in code that was fine, while the memory that mattered was sitting in a directory.

articles.title: I Trimmed My Agent's Tool Results to Five Fields. It Solved More, Not Fewer.
articles.description: A reader named izgorodin left a comment on my piece about the 200-tool menu, and it changed the...
articles.body_html:
A reader named izgorodin left a comment on my piece about the 200-tool menu, and it changed the question I thought I was answering. He had run the numbers himself: forty turns of a triage helper whose only tool returns five GitHub issues, and by turn twenty the tool results were 99.1 percent of everything sent, about 326,000 tokens, thirteen times the cost of the menu itself. Keeping only the last six turns flattened the call at around 99,000. Trimming each result to the five fields the helper actually reads kept the whole history and ended turn forty at 36,934. Then he wrote the sentence that matters: his replay called no model and used a fixed answer, so it measured how big the window gets, not whether the helper still finds what it needs.

That is the question I spent this week answering. Same twelve triage jobs, run twice: once with the full issue text coming back, once with each result cut to the five fields (the number, the title, the labels, the comment count, and the first 300 characters of the body). A real model did the work, a small one I run locally, and every job was scored on whether it found the right issue and the right label. I expected the trim to cost something. I was wrong about the direction.

My claim before the numbers: trimming the results would save about half the tokens per turn and cost a few solved jobs, because sooner or later the helper would need something the trim cut. The first half was right. The second half was backwards.

Problem 1: the trim did not cost a single solved job

Across both runs, the full results solved 9 of 24 jobs. The trimmed results solved 17 of 24. That is 37.5 percent against 70.8, and the gap is not a rounding error in one direction: the trim won 9 to 4 in the first run and 8 to 5 in the second. Look at the twelve jobs one by one and the trim never loses a job the full text wins. The two arms agree on seven jobs (both solve four, both fail three), and on the other five the trim wins or ties every time.

Three jobs beat the model in both arms, and they are worth naming because they set the limit. On the Linux dependency guide, the Windows 11 question, and the misspelled error dialog, the model answered the crash-on-launch issue every single time, in both arms, in both runs. Those are small-model limits, not trim damage. The trim cannot be blamed for what the full text also fails, and the fact that the failures are identical in both arms is the cleanest evidence in the whole run that the trim is not hiding anything load-bearing.

Problem 2: the full text has a favourite issue, and it is always the crash

The full arm's failures have a shape, and once you see it you cannot unsee it. On five of its failed jobs, the model answered issue 412, the crash on launch, with the label "bug" — whatever the job actually asked. The job about garbled dates in a CSV export? 412, bug. The job about the install guide missing a Linux step? 412, bug. The job about a typo in an error dialog? 412, bug. It even went back and read 412 a second time before answering it, as if checking its work.

The trimmed arm does the same second look just as often, about once per job in both arms, but it answers the right issue afterwards. The difference is not that the trim hides the crash report. It is that five short results sit side by side and all five stay visible, while five long ones let the most dramatic report swallow the rest. A small model reading a long list does not weigh five issues. It remembers the loudest one. Cutting the noise did not just save tokens. It changed what the model could pay attention to, and attention was the scarce thing, not information.

Problem 3: the full text can eat the whole window just by looping

The ugliest full-arm result is not a wrong answer. It is no answer at all. On two jobs the model listed the issues, listed them again, and listed them again, six turns of the same call, and burned 10,063 tokens on one job before the turn cap stopped it. The first time I ran this, that loop pushed the prompt past the model's whole window and the run died outright. I added a rule that a repeated call comes back as a one-line note instead of the full dump again, the same rule in both arms, and the run survived, but the loop still cost the job.

The trimmed arm never needed a fourth turn on any job. Every job ended in three: list, one second look, answer. The full arm averaged close to four turns and needed six on its worst jobs, and each of those extra turns carried another thousand-plus tokens of history with it. The token bill per turn tells the same story from the other side. Turn one is identical in both arms, about 179 tokens. Turn two is 1,749 with full results and 759 trimmed. By the third turn the full arm is sending about 1,900 tokens a turn and the trimmed arm about 1,080. The average across the run is 1,421 tokens per turn against 673, and 5,475 per job against 2,020. The trim cuts the bill by more than half per turn and almost two thirds per job, and the jobs it saves are the ones where the full text was already losing.

Problem 4: the second look is not the price of the trim

izgorodin asked for a miss signal alongside the solved rate, and he was right to: a trim that quietly sends the helper back for the full text every time has not saved anything, it has just moved the cost. So I counted every time the helper asked for one issue in full. Full results: 0.88 second looks per job. Trimmed results: 0.92. That is the same number, inside the wobble between runs, and it is the number that surprised me most. The trim did not drive the helper back for more. The helper goes back about once per job in both arms, usually to look once more at the issue it is about to answer, and the full text costs the same second look for the same reason.

That kills the natural objection in both directions. The trim is not free because the helper never needs the cut material: it goes back just as often. And it is not expensive because of the second looks, because the second looks cost the same either way. The saving is in the list itself, paid once per turn, and the second look is a fixed cost of doing the job carefully, not a tax on trimming.

Problem 5: the honest limit is the size of the model

All of this is one small model on twelve jobs. A bigger model would solve more jobs in both arms (the three jobs that beat this one in both arms would probably fall), and the gap between the arms would likely shrink. The absolute rates, 38 percent and 71 percent, belong to this model and these twelve jobs, and anyone quoting them as general truths about agents is over-reading a small run. Twelve jobs is also small enough that the run-to-run wobble is a whole job per arm. I ran it twice for that reason, and the direction held in both runs, but the direction is the finding, not the percentages.

The other limit is the jobs themselves. My issue bodies run a hundred-odd words, shorter than real reports. Real bodies are longer, messier, and more repetitive, which would widen the token gap, not narrow it. But it would also give the trim more to cut, and I have not measured that. The five fields are also izgorodin's five, chosen for a triage prompt that cites numbers and suggests one existing label. A different prompt reads different fields, and its trim would cut somewhere else.

So the rule I am keeping is narrower than the one I went in with. Trim the result to the fields the prompt actually reads, and measure the solved rate before you argue about it, because the cost you expect (the helper going back for what you cut) may not exist, and the benefit you did not expect (the helper deciding better with less noise) may be the whole story. The menu was never the bill. The results were. And the results, it turns out, were also the distraction.

What do you trim from your tool results, and did you check whether the solved rate moved when you did? I would like to hear the number, either way, and what the helper went back for when it went back.

P.S. Everything I write stays free — that part doesn't change. But if this one was worth something to you, you can buy me a coffee ☕ (one-time or monthly, both work). It covers the API credits and hosting behind these experiments — and honestly, it's also the nudge that gets the next one started on the evenings I'd otherwise skip it. — Salam

articles.title: WebRTC file transfer with a 9-digit code and no signaling server of my own
articles.description: I built File Transfer, a tool that sends files directly between two browsers. One screen shows a...
articles.body_html:
I built File Transfer, a tool that sends files directly between two browsers. One screen shows a 9-digit code (for example 482-915-736), the other side types it in, and the two devices connect peer-to-peer over WebRTC. Files never touch a server.

  • Web version (nothing to install): https://rentabextension-oss.github.io/rentab/ft/?utm_source=devto
  • Chrome extension (side panel): https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/lffomfhccijamechladimcfcpijpjnne?utm_source=devto

In this post I want to show the part I found most interesting: how to connect two browsers safely with only a short code, without running a signaling server.

The big picture

To open a WebRTC connection, the two sides first have to exchange an offer and an answer (SDP) somehow. Usually you run your own signaling server for that. Here I use public Nostr relays and public MQTT brokers as a "bulletin board", and everything posted there is encrypted.

Device A (shows code)        Public relays (Nostr / MQTT)        Device B (types code)
        | -- p1: CPace share Ya ----------------> |                       |
        |                                         | <-- p2: Yb + encrypted offer
        | -- p3: encrypted answer ---------------> |                       |
        | ======== direct WebRTC (DTLS) connection, files go P2P ======== |

The relays only ever see a few short encrypted messages. File contents never pass through them.

What's inside the 9-digit code

482-915-736 has two parts:

Part Role Leaves the device?
482 (first 3 digits) picks a "mailbox" on the relays yes (not secret)
915-736 (last 6 digits) the CPace password never

The first 3 digits are hashed before being used as a topic name:

const topicFor = async (np: string) =>
  [...(await sha('p2pft-nameplate|' + np))]
    .slice(0, 20)
    .map((b) => b.toString(16).padStart(2, '0'))
    .join('');

On Nostr, messages are ephemeral events (kind 25050, a range relays don't store) tagged with #t; on MQTT they are published to p2pft/<topic>.

Why a PAKE (CPace) and not "encrypt with the code"

The simplest idea is "derive a key from the 6 digits and encrypt the offer with it". That's dangerous: 6 digits are only a million combinations, so anyone watching the relay could grab the ciphertext and brute-force it offline.

So I use CPace, a PAKE, on ristretto255:

  • both sides run Diffie-Hellman with a generator derived from the password
  • they only end up with the same key if the passwords match
  • an eavesdropper can't test passwords offline from what they saw

If someone types a wrong code, the keys don't match, decryption fails, and the host throws that code away (a bad message). So each code allows exactly one guess. Codes also rotate every 10 minutes.

After connecting, both screens show four words derived from both DTLS fingerprints (for example clock · ferry · hazel · spider). If anything had been swapped in the middle, the words would differ.

Making both sides land on the same relays

Public relays are often down, so the app connects to several from a long list at once. But when each side picked randomly, they sometimes had no relay in common and never met (about 1 in 6 times).

The fix: a shuffle seeded by the topic. Same code → same order → same relays on both sides.

function shuffle<T>(a: T[], seed: string): T[] {
  let h = 2166136261 >>> 0; // FNV-1a
  for (let i = 0; i < seed.length; i++) h = Math.imul(h ^ seed.charCodeAt(i), 16777619) >>> 0;
  const rnd = () => { h ^= h << 13; h >>>= 0; h ^= h >>> 17; h ^= h << 5; h >>>= 0; return h; };
  const r = [...a];
  for (let i = r.length - 1; i > 0; i--) {
    const j = rnd() % (i + 1);
    [r[i], r[j]] = [r[j], r[i]];
  }
  return r;
}

Nostr and MQTT run in parallel, and either one is enough. If no relay gets through, the app falls back to a mode where the two people copy a long code to each other by hand.

Shrinking the SDP

A raw SDP is several KB. What's really needed is the DTLS fingerprint, the ICE ufrag/pwd and a few candidate addresses, so only those are packed into a compact binary form. New candidate types (for example relay candidates from the user's own TURN server) reuse the existing format so older versions stay compatible.

The transfer itself

  • files are split into 1 MB blocks, each checked with SHA-256
  • the receiver writes to OPFS from a worker, so memory stays flat
  • after a drop, the transfer resumes from the first missing block
  • the send buffer is paced with bufferedAmountLowThreshold
  • on high-latency links one DataChannel stalls, so up to 8 extra RTCPeerConnections are added, and kept only if they actually help
  • on-the-fly zstd compression (WebAssembly), with the level re-tuned every 2 seconds to match the line speed

When it doesn't work

There's no TURN server in the design, so some networks can't connect. From anonymous stats (no IP addresses are collected) the three main causes are:

  1. symmetric NAT on both sides: neither can accept an incoming connection
  2. Wi-Fi client isolation: same network, but devices aren't allowed to talk to each other
  3. CGNAT: the ISP shares one public address between many customers

The app runs a quick network check before connecting and explains the cause when it can. Settings also let you add your own TURN server, and when a phone and a computer are next to each other, the app suggests connecting the computer to the phone's hotspot.

Takeaways

  • public Nostr / MQTT can work as a bulletin board, so WebRTC can connect without your own signaling server
  • if you use a short code, don't turn it into a key directly: use a PAKE (CPace)
  • with public relays, pick them deterministically so both sides choose the same ones

The web version works without installing anything. I'd love to hear whether it connects on your network and what speed you get.

  • Web: https://rentabextension-oss.github.io/rentab/ft/?utm_source=devto
  • Chrome extension: https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/lffomfhccijamechladimcfcpijpjnne?utm_source=devto

articles.title: My Tank Bot Kept Winning Fights and Losing Games — 10 Versions of Debugging battle.training
articles.description: My bot kimmy won 94% of its local test games, died live from a pathfinding bug, plateaued, got worse after a "fix", and is still ranked ~200th. Here's the honest version history, with the replay numbers.
articles.body_html:
My Tank Bot Kept Winning Fights and Losing Games — 10 Versions of Debugging battle.training

My bot is called kimmy. It plays battle.training — a tank-commander arena where you write a controller, it fights other people's controllers on a ladder, and the November Cup pays $250 in USDC to the top 3.

As of this morning, kimmy sits at rank 203 of 347 on the public ladder (rating 1150) and rank 148 of 266 in the November Cup (rating 1147, 214 games played). The cup leaders are at 1720, 1629, and 1591. So no, this is not a victory lap. This is the debugging log of a bot that kept finding new ways to lose — and what each version actually taught me.

The game in 60 seconds

Each side drafts a small squad — mine is MBT + APC + drone + scout — and the match is won by hill points or elimination. Hills (objectives) score points per tick while you hold them, and the APC is the only unit with capture weight 2, so it scores double on a hill. Your controller is one JavaScript file with a tick() function that issues orders every tick, inside a 40-unit tick budget. Blow the budget and your units get no orders at all — they just sit there while the enemy shoots them.

That last detail is the whole story of v7.

v1–v4: learning to walk

The early versions were smoke tests with ideas attached: basic navigation, a holder-stays rule, missile closing in to re-acquire targets, drone fleeing at 32 tiles. v1 lost 0–2 to panel-holder. v3 lost 0–2 to kilnwarden in a ruin-trap game that took a full diagnosis to understand. v4 drew with erine-vanguard and blackbox-d542. v7 — the version with flow-field navigation — beat tsugi 2–0, the same bot that had beaten v2 2–0. Progress felt real.

v5–v7: the BFS death

v5 and v6 were rejected by the smoke test before they ever saw a ranked game: 10–11% tick failures. v7 passed the smoke test (6% failures) and looked great locally — 146–14 (91.25%) against the four house bots. Then it played live.

Live, v7 collapsed: public rank 197, rating 1123, cup record 5W-7L-4D. Replay analysis of the two worst losses showed why: the controller was running a breadth-first search at runtime, and one BFS costs about 41 units — the entire tick budget. On the failure seeds, v7 racked up 4,300+ null-order ticks: whole stretches of the game where every unit stood still, doing nothing, while the enemy took the hills.

The lesson was brutal and simple: a controller that is smart 95% of the time and frozen 5% of the time loses to a dumber controller that never freezes.

v8: kill the BFS, find the plateau

v8 removed runtime BFS entirely. Navigation became flow fields built once in hello() plus a drive-straight fallback, so tick() could never blow its budget on pathfinding. Locally it was the best version yet: 151–9 (94.4%). On the exact v7 death seeds, null-order ticks went from 4,300+ to zero.

Live, v8 worked — and then it stopped working. The cup rating plateaued around 1143–1160, rank ~119–128. The diagnosis, from the last 36 cup sets, was not a bug: kimmy won fights but lost on points. 28 of 36 losses ended hill_locked versus only 7 by elimination. The draft had no APC, and the APC is the only unit with capture weight 2 — an enemy APC sitting on a hill scores 6 points a tick against our scout's or MBT's 3. We were outscoring ourselves.

v9: the APC fix that made things worse

v9-C drafted the APC (MBT + APC + drone + scout) and added six fixes: clear-the-contest, a stale-memory timeout, missile/drone as second cappers, phased spreading, and an early hill race. Locally: 149–11 (93.1%). In scrimmages it beat both nemeses 2–0 — wowok, and blucca-goalkeeper, a four-APC bot v8 had never beaten.

Then it played 40 ranked sets. 9W-15L-16D — worse than v8's 12W-10L-14D over its last 36. The replay diagnosis was deeper than the v8 one: the MBT and APC were freezing on hills we already held (capture is max, not sum — the extra unit adds zero points), and firing into terrain. The deepest finding came from a switchyard replay: the enemy APC sat 6 tiles away behind a height-245 ridge while kimmy shot from height ~205 — every shell grounded out on the ridge. And the navigation shortcut that suppressed replans within 8 tiles of a goal had wedged units against a rock wall for 3,500 ticks.

v10: shoot the denier, not the drone

v10 — deployed 17 Nov, still active — is six fixes aimed at exactly those failures:

  1. Designated holder: a unit stays on a held hill only if it is the best holder there. Scout holds light hills, APC holds the heaviest, MBT only when it's the sole holder.
  2. MBT closes onto hills: if its target sits on an objective we don't hold, the MBT drives onto that objective's centre instead of shooting from a stand-off.
  3. Shoot the denier: on a contested hill, every unit's shared target is the enemy unit on that hill.
  4. Clear to the hill, not the tile: a clearer drives to the contested hill's centre; a unit already inside stays and shoots.
  5. The denier is the APC, not the nearest drone: the target is picked by capture weight first, then lowest HP — v9 had been burning DPS on 30-HP drones while the 110-HP APC denying the hill survived untouched (355 shots in one game, APC at full HP).
  6. Clear-shot repositioning and Nav replan when wedged: the controller replicates the shell-arc check from the map heights, so a unit with no clear shot flanks instead of firing into a ridge — and a blocked unit replans even near its goal.

Local test: 149–11 (93.1%), zero tick errors. The counterfactuals — re-simulating real lost replays with v10 swapped in — flipped a fit50 loss into a win by elimination and turned a 0–19987 switchyard loss into a live game at 10196–19797. Live scrimmages were more honest: lost 0–2 to fit50-bot (but by 2,900 and 1,895 points instead of 8,460), drew 1–1 with wizard-tank, which v9 had lost 0–2 to. v10 fixes the specific failures proven in the replays. It does not make kimmy a champion.

Where it stands now

All numbers verified live this morning (19 Nov 2026) from the battle.training API:

Public ladder November Cup
Rank 203 / 347 148 / 266
Rating 1150 1147
Games 59 sets (20W-20L-19D) 214 games (58W-65L-91D)
Score 1061 1097
Version v10 v10

The qualification bar for the cup — 100 ranked sets — was cleared on 17 Nov. The rating bar that matters for the BOT BOUNTY is "above house-starter": house-starter sits at 725 on the public ladder and 879 in the cup, so kimmy clears it on both. The top 3 (1720 / 1629 / 1591) is still hundreds of points away, and with the cup closing 30 Nov, that's the honest distance.

What ten versions actually taught me

  • A frozen controller loses more games than a dumb one. The tick budget is a hard constraint, not a performance hint. v7's 91% local win rate meant nothing live.
  • Winning fights is not winning games. v8 proved it: 28 of 36 losses on hill points. Scoreboard first, kills second.
  • Local tests lie about the meta. House bots never draft APC and never hide behind ridges, so local tests can't measure the fixes that matter most against real opponents. Counterfactual replays — re-simulating a real loss with the new version — were the only validation that predicted live behavior.
  • Every "fix" needs its own replay diagnosis. v9 fixed v8's problem and created a worse one. The only way to know was to watch the replays and count: real order percentage per unit, shots fired, shells grounded on terrain.

The bot is still playing 24/7, and v10's next twenty ranked sets will say more about it than this post can. You can watch it live at battle.training/bots/kimmy.

Disclosure: I built this bot, and I'm submitting this post for battle.training's BOT BOUNTY ($15) on promotedby.ai — the bounty asks for a post that names the bot and links its page, once the bot has played 100 ranked sets and is rated above house-starter. Both conditions are met, and the numbers above are from the live API.

articles.title: My tests were green. They caught 0 of 10 real bugs.
articles.description: I had a small web shop with four end-to-end tests. All four passed, every time. I felt good about...
articles.body_html:
I had a small web shop with four end-to-end tests. All four passed, every time. I felt good about them.

Then I broke the shop on purpose, ten different ways, and ran the same four tests against each broken version. They caught zero.

That's the problem I built Saboteur to measure: a green suite tells you nothing about what it misses. I built it for the KaneCLI Online Hackathon by TestMu AI.

Live report: https://softalpha0.github.io/saboteur/
Code: https://github.com/softalpha0/saboteur

The idea in one paragraph

Saboteur plants one small, realistic bug at a time, builds the app, and runs your test suite against it. If every test still passes, the bug "slipped". For each bug that slipped, Claude writes a new test, and the test is only kept if it passes on the correct app and fails on the bugged one. No test gets in on the model's word alone.
